content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released updated recommendations for the treatment of adolescents and children with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, as well as guidance on simplified service delivery and diagnostics for HCV. These updates are accompanied by a summary of declarations of conflicts of interest from contributors involved in the guideline development process, as outlined in Web Annex A. The publication is available under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. WHO does not endorse any specific organizations, products, or services, and the use of its logo is prohibited. If the work is adapted, it must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the work must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The publication includes a general disclaimer that the designations and presentation of material do not imply any opinion from WHO regarding the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. WHO does not endorse specific companies or products mentioned in the publication. While all reasonable precautions have been taken to verify the information, the material is distributed without warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. WHO is not liable for any damages arising from the use of the material. The guideline development process included a review of potential conflicts of interest among contributors. Significant declarations of interest are summarized as follows: 1. Jason Grebely: Declared research support from Cephied (USD 300,000), Gilead Sciences (USD 1,500,000), and Hologic (USD 250,000) as part of National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Partnership Project grants in Australia, where he serves as the chief investigator. These grants include in-kind contributions such as cartridges and platforms valued at USD 5 million from Cephied and HCV RNA tests valued at USD 150,000 from Hologic. Non-monetary support valued at over USD 1,000 was also declared, including contributions from AbbVie (USD 5,000 in 2020), Cephied (USD 3,000 in 2020), and Gilead Sciences (USD 3,000 in 2021). Action taken: Partial exclusion from voting on the HCV point-of-care viral load topic, with contributions limited to expert input or presentations. 2. Christian B. Ramers: Declared consulting fees from AbbVie (USD 1,500) for participation in the Targeted HCV Elimination Steering Committee. Research support was declared for a pragmatic clinical trial (STAT program) funded by Gilead Sciences (USD 637,500), which involves mobile HCV treatment for people who inject drugs. The grant was received by his institution, but he is not directly involved in the project or in receipt of funds. Additional declarations include participation in HCV speakers’ bureaus for Gilead Sciences (USD 2,000) and AbbVie (USD 2,000). Action taken: Declared interests were deemed not in conflict with the guideline development topics. 3. Lai Wei: Declared consulting fees from Gilead (USD 1,000 in 2020), Huahui (USD 2,000 in 2021), MSD (USD 500 in 2019), and Pfizer (USD 1,000 in 2021). Speaker fees were declared from Asclitis (USD 500 in 2020), BMS (USD 500 in 2018), Gilead (USD 500 in 2018, 2019, and 2020), and Kayin (USD 1,000 in 2020). Research grants were declared from AbbVie (USD 100,000 from 2017–2019 for strengthening patient management databases), BMS (USD 100,000 from 2015–2018 for HCV genotyping in China), and Gilead (USD 200,000 in 2021 for developing an algorithm to support linkage to care following testing in 50 hospitals). Only one active project, the linkage-to-care project, is ongoing and is not tied to any specific company’s drugs. The publication is part of WHO’s efforts to provide transparent and evidence-based recommendations for improving HCV care and treatment globally.
